plausibleAlternatives: nitrogen, magnesium, iron, sulfur, potassium, or another deficiency, antagonism, excess, pH, or EC problem
underwatering, overwatering, root disease, low oxygen, heat, cold, light, or transplant stress

mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Identify species, expected deciduous or production-stage behavior, tissue age and position, season and photoperiod; map old versus new tissue and affected versus unaffected plants; inspect roots, pests, lesions and vascular signs; measure root-zone and environmental conditions; and document marked-leaf progression and new-growth health before classifying yellowing as normal.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: routine observation is appropriate for expected seasonal or stage-linked color change, but rapid off-season spread, young-growth symptoms, wilting, lesions, or vascular decline requires prompt investigation
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Do not quarantine for expected senescence or fallen leaves alone; use pest or disease precautions only when transmissible evidence or progressive patterns support them.
expectedScoutingSteps: capture whole plants, canopy position, old and new leaves, veins, stems, roots, fallen tissue, nearby plants, and affected-unaffected comparisons
record species, deciduous behavior, crop stage, harvest or reproduction timing, season, photoperiod, temperature trend, frost, irrigation, and recent inputs
inspect for pests, eggs, frass, lesions, pathogen structures, vascular discoloration, root decay, residue, and spray or drift patterns
mark leaves and track color, abscission, spread, and new-growth health while measuring moisture, pH, EC, and method-appropriate nutrient or tissue context
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Treat senescence as a timing-and-distribution diagnosis, not a synonym for yellow leaves. Require species and stage, tissue age, season or harvest context, old-versus-new distribution, roots, environment, progression, and exclusion of pests, disease, nutrition, pH, EC, water, spray, and camera effects; preserve uncertainty when detached leaves lack source context and avoid reflex feeding or treatment.

record fertilizer, amendment, foliar, irrigation, runoff, drainage, environmental, and crop-stage history

mediaRecords.lifeStage: mature container plant and established field crop in separate observations
mediaRecords.affectedLocation: exposed root systems without paired young leaves, growing points, fruit, flowers, stems, root-zone measurements, or symptomatic controls
mediaRecords.distribution: cross-host root examples without container, row, depth, irrigation, canopy, or affected-unaffected distribution from one case
mediaRecords.progression: single-time references without root development trend, young-tissue symptoms, transpiration history, correction response, or recovery
mediaRecords.mediumRootZone: root density and field-root context are visible, but moisture, oxygen, temperature, pH, EC, calcium availability, salinity, compaction, drainage, and usable volume are not measured
mediaRecords.environment: humidity, VPD, airflow, leaf temperature, irrigation, rainfall, transpiration demand, and growth rate are absent

diagnosticSigns: the root-bound spider plant caption explicitly notes that the plant remained healthy, flowered, and produced runners
visible root density does not establish calcium deficiency or impaired uptake
calcium-related young-tissue symptoms require separation of supply, root function, water movement, transpiration, growth rate, and local tissue demand
plausibleAlternatives: healthy root density or normal mature container occupancy without disorder
restricted volume, compaction, low oxygen, waterlogging, drought, damaged roots, root disease, or root pests
pH, EC, salinity, alkalinity, nutrient antagonism, excess, or actual calcium shortage
high or low VPD, poor airflow, heat, cold, rapid growth, irregular irrigation, or local transpiration limitation
boron or other nutrient disorder, spray injury, disease, pests, genetics, or physical damage
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Pair sharp young-tissue and affected-organ views with washed roots and unaffected controls; measure moisture, oxygen context, pH, EC, temperature, usable root volume, irrigation delivery, humidity or VPD, airflow and growth rate; review nutrient and alkalinity history; and obtain method-appropriate solution, medium or tissue testing before attributing symptoms to calcium supply or uptake.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: inspect active young-tissue, fruit, flower, or growing-point injury and root function promptly while avoiding blind calcium addition
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Do not quarantine for root density or suspected calcium-uptake disorder alone; isolate only when separate evidence supports a transmissible root, pest, or disease cause.
expectedScoutingSteps: capture whole plants, young and old tissue, growing points, fruit or flowers, stems, washed roots, containers or field zones, and matched affected-unaffected controls
measure root-zone moisture, oxygen context, temperature, pH, EC, drainage, usable volume and irrigation delivery plus humidity or VPD, airflow and leaf temperature
record calcium and complete nutrient inputs, water alkalinity, salinity, amendments, growth rate, crop load, transplant and root-disturbance history
obtain method-appropriate solution, medium, water or tissue testing and track new growth after one reviewed root-zone or environment correction
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Do not infer calcium deficiency from root density, distorted young tissue, blossom-end symptoms, or one root photo. Separate nutrient supply from pH or EC availability, root function, water movement, VPD and airflow, rapid growth, local tissue demand, disease, pests, and physical restriction; require measurements and method-appropriate testing; and avoid automatic calcium, flushing, irrigation, or repotting directions.
